utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you there during the evening hours, late afternoon/early evening hours, on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether Colonel Blagojevic was around the Bratunac area on that particular day, the 18th, the 19th, those days?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No. I received the order from Major Eskic, not from Blagojevic, so no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if I understand your testimony correctly, it was only one day that you searched the terrain. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On that particular day, you indicated there was Mico Gavric and a gentleman named Jevic, and then some 30 to 40 prisoners who were captured. Could you tell us whether among those prisoners, whether there were any children, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, to the best of your knowledge, what happened to those children.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: The children remained in the area just above the road near water. When I went there for the last time, the children were having dinner, which had been given to them by Mico Gavric. And they remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know who was responsible or who took responsibility for the children?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: From my point of view, it should have been Mico Gavric, as the coordinator representing the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now -- again, just to make sure I understand or to make sure that we have it in the record, when was it that you left for Zepa?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date. Perhaps it might have been the 20th, 21st. But anyway, it was in the evening hours and Colonel Blagojevic greeted us up there, but I'm not sure of the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, from the period of time that Srebrenica fell, that would be 11 July 1995 to the time that you left for Zepa, did you or your men come across any prisoners at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Except for the 18th, not on any other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's when we're talking about the searching of the terrain with Mr. Jevic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the Prosecution has contended that the Serb officers got together and planned the execution of all the men that they could get their hands on among the able-bodied men that were either in Potocari or that they could capture later in the field. Were you at any time given any orders or did you ever become aware of any orders or any such plan that you were to capture and execute any Muslims that you could get your hands on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Not me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of your men, whether they had orders or otherwise, or otherwise, in light of what had been going on in that area for the last three or four years, do you know if any of your men were engaged in any atrocities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we have a report by one of the employees of the Office of the Prosecution. He's no longer with them, but he was working with them, and he made a report. And he indicates that there is a particular soldier by the name of Slavoljub Grujicic, as a member of the 3rd Battalion. Was he by any chance, to your recollection, a member of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, just to make sure, let me show you what is being marked for identification purposes as D143. And I should note for the record that translation is pending.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This was a document that we obtained from the Office of the Prosecution, and it's a roster.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I believe I've designated an area for you to look at in order to --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see the name of Slavoljub Grujicic? I believe I'm pronouncing the name correctly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell us whether according to this roster provided to us by the Office of the Prosecution dated July 1995, whether this individual was a member of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you were in Banja Luka, I believe they did show you a photograph of a gentleman by the name of Tanasijevic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he was in front of an APC smoking. They caught him just in the moment when he was taking a big drag.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was he a member of your -- of the 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Had you given him any orders to go anywhere with that APC, you specifically? Had you given him any orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: On the 12th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And where was he on his way to? Where was he going?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: When they were leaving, that is to say, the other equipment, he went to Bratunac, too. The APC was faulty, the caterpillar part, track, was faulty, so he was taken it to Bratunac to be repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take it if it needed to be repaired, it had some problems with it. Would you please describe to us to the best of your recollection the working condition of this APC, this ominous-looking piece of machinery.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: It was an APC, an armoured personnel carrier. It was the first official armoured carrier. It was 1995. And it was a vehicle that was 35 years old. When the events in Srebrenica were taking place, it did not take part in any combat operations; it wasn't used for that. And I came across it at Pribicevac. And I think it served for morale boosting rather than combat operations, because it wasn't capable of being used for manoeuvres and speedy movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, if it was capable of morale boosting, its appearance itself would have some ominous effect on those who were on the receiving end of viewing that APC, would it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: As to the other side, the opposite side, it wasn't able to see it, except its reconnoitering units, if they used units of that kind because it wasn't to the forefront; it was in the back facing downwards. So it wasn't actually visible from that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But the Prosecution's theory is that it was sent there, whether it was operational or not, it was sent there, at least by its mere presence, that in and of itself would have this -- would cause this fear on those who were viewing it, such as the people from Srebrenica who were leaving towards Potocari. So my question is: Was it sent there -- was it sent to Potocari to have some sort of a -- an effect on the Muslim citizens of Srebrenica that were leaving and going to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No. No, I explained this question in Banja Luka. And if necessary, I can explain it again briefly. It happened quite by chance. From Pribicevac it was going to Sase, Pobrdje, Bratunac. So on the 12th when it was returning to Bratunac to be repaired, it wasn't -- it didn't use the Potocari/Bratunac/Srebrenica communication at all, or road. It used the Pribicevac/Sase/Bjelovac Road, Pobrdje, Bratunac, so that it was used along the route that we took to reach our positions. And after it was repaired, it was supposed to go on the 13th, that is to say, when we were at Bojna, the APC was supposed to appear at Bojna, since the caterpillar section was taken off very quickly. It just takes a couple of minutes. On the 13th - and actually I talked later on to them, there was a mistake. And on the 13th, they were told, you don't have to go right round, take a roundabout route, you can go to Srebrenica by Potocari and climb up to Bojna. So this was a mistake, lack of information, and it was because of that that it started up that route, in that direction. There wasn't any purpose to it, or intent, it just happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to move to another section. I have a couple of matters left, just some clean-up matters we talked earlier about the Red Berets. First of all, I will be handing you what has been marked for identification purposes as D141. And before we get to this document itself, if you could please tell us, who is -- who are the Red Berets responsible to? You told us that there was one or two platoons or one platoon I believe that was attached to the 3rd Battalion. Was there another platoon of Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, from August 1994, since the death of their commander, Bosko, the company was divided half and half, into two platoons. One platoon was led by Brodonovic Prodanovic. I forget his first name. And the second platoon was led by Rade Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, were they attached -- both of these platoons, were they permanently or temporarily or occasionally attached to the 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: The platoon led by Rade Petrovic was just from June to July, so for those 10 or 15 days, in actual fact attached. But according to my information, it was attached at that point in time when the forces of the BH army launched a classical ambush by coming out of the zone and killing six policemen, 3 kilometres in front of the UN forces in front of the Zeleni Jadar/Kragivoda communication line or road. And at that time, the Red Beret platoon was sent from Bratunac to, as we say in the army, to pull out the dead. There weren't any wounded because all of them were killed, so they were sent to pull out the dead. And as my battalion was about 37 or 8 kilometres away from Bratunac at that distance, the arrival of these forces was an additional time. And they didn't actually mean anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Who sent them, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Probably the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So can we say that the Red Berets were members of the Bratunac Brigade? Were they official members of the Bratunac Brigade? Let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Of the Bratunac Brigade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you spoke about the one platoon. What about the other platoon?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: The other platoon was never in that terrain, and I think that at that point in time it was not in Bratunac either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's look at -- just incidentally, there was -- one name has popped up, an individual who was taken to the hospital, I believe killed, in the afternoon of 13 July 1995. It says in Kravica. Slavoljub Mladjenovic -- no, that's not him. I'm sorry. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe the person is -- was killed. He was, in fact, wounded and just not to mischaracterise the facts. And also, the question is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman by the name of I believe it's Stanojevic? The Prosecution claims that he was killed in -- or he was injured in the Kravica warehouse atrocity on the afternoon of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, that's a very leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not leading at all. I asked him if he knows the gentleman. It's a fact that the Prosecution over and over and over again has suggested that the --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think you could leave the second part of the question and just ask a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I was putting my case to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you tell us: Do you know this individual?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at D141, the document that I just handed you. All right. Do you -- could you please tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: The handover of weapons and ammunition from the Crvene Beretke warehouse to the 3rd Infantry Battalion warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what is the date, sir, on this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: The date is the 18th of January, in the typed-out text, and in the handwritten text it says the 31st of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you see your signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You recognise it as being your signature, not somebody signing your name for you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So that is your signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, what does this document mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: I think that at the time what happened was -- well, probably the difference is in the dates. On the 18th of January, I was not there, I was probably around Trnovo, in the Trnovo area, and I probably signed the document on the 31st of January. I think that's what happened. But this is yet another piece of evidence showing that the Red Berets were not composition of the 3rd Infantry Battalion, that they had their own warehouses and their own command, and that they kept that throughout that time. Probably this handover took place when it took place; that's not being challenged. And I assume they could have turned this over to the 1st Battalion or the 2nd Battalion. That's not the important point. They decided upon the 3rd Battalion probably because the commander or rather the komandir and my deputy were related, actually they were father and son. Now, the combat operations had ceased after the signing of the Dayton Accord, so that in principle that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that one point is crystal clear. You said that there was some significance with respect to the two warehouses, if I understand you correctly, that the Red Berets had --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- theirs and the 3rd Battalion had their own. Now, why is that significant? Why should we care at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Well, the only important thing, as far as I see it, is if somebody insists upon the fact that the Red Berets belonged exclusively to the 3rd Battalion, to the 3rd Infantry Battalion. Only in that context would it be significance. Otherwise, in any other context, I can't see what this would be. But if somebody has a specific question, I should be happy to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me be a little more precise. Why are you suggesting, rather emphatically, might I say, that the Red Berets were not part of the 3rd Battalion? What is in this document that at least gives credence to your observations or your beliefs that the Red Berets were not part of the 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Because it supplies from their warehouse, the warehouse of the Red Berets into the warehouse of the 3rd Infantry Battalion. So since they were established in 1992, they were an independent autonomous unit. And I draw that conclusion from this context. When you were reading the order from Mr. Blagojevic, in fact, where it states auxiliary forces to attack and so on and so forth, so in that context -- otherwise, the Red Berets as Red Berets, per se, I don't have any bad information about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Quite simply, let me make this clear once again, that they weren't within the composition of the 3rd Infantry Battalion. That is to say, they were not under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to show you one last document, a document dated July 4, 1994. Were you a member of the Bratunac Brigade during this period, 4 July 1994?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When did you become a member of the -- just refresh our memories again. When did you become --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: In mid-February 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's when you returned from military academy, the schooling?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No. I completed my schooling on the 20th of June, 1994. And after that, I went to the 1st Guard's. Three months later, I was wounded on the 1st of October, 1994. And until February, I was undergoing treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: And I continued my treatment in May and June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So there was this gap when you were not with the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you came back to the Bratunac Brigade, were you informed that there was this policy that was based on this information, drafted by the previous commander of the Bratunac Brigade, a Lieutenant Colonel Ognjenovic, and that you were to carry out this particular policy? Were you informed of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did your newly arrived commander, Colonel Blagojevic, when he came did he ever rally the troops, rally the commanders and tell them that he was going to carry on the policies set out in this information piece by Mr. -- by Lieutenant Colonel Ognjenovic? Did he ever say any such thing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware prior to coming here today that this document existed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How is that? You are a commander of a battalion. How can you possibly not know that Lieutenant Colonel Ognjenovic drafted this very important information sheet that the Prosecution is anchoring part of their theory of the Prosecution? How can you not know that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: It's clearly not necessary, the latter part of Mr. Karnavas's question, and it's very, very leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Absolutely, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was my last question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, by the way, Mr. Karnavas. Would you for the sake of the record, would you tell us the identification number of this document, just for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The very famous one, the 4 July 1994, that's D132.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Without the last part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll try to edit myself, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How is it, how is it, that you don't know about this document? Can you explain it to us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Well, during that period of time I wasn't there. I'm not sure whether it existed in the archives of the battalion that I inherited, and that article that I saw I don't know how far it is realistic. If the United Nations had normal communication and normal channels of bringing in food, Medicines sans frontiers were entering Srebrenica, I really don't know. I have no definition, no explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I really appreciate your answers. Mr. Stojanovic may have some questions; he represents Mr. Jokic. I'm sure the Prosecution will have some questions, as may the Judges. If you could be as honest and forthright with them as you have been with me, I would appreciate it. Thank you for coming here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, do you think you have any questions to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, Mr. Zekic. Our Defence team has no questions for this witness, in view of his testimony here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, we haven't received the witness list for the next week. If it is prepared, could we be furnished during the break or this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it should have been furnished, Your Honour, but probably the troops were waiting for the commander to look over the final order. So I will make sure that we will have it for you, perhaps as early as when we come back from the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the rule we have been working on is two weeks, so if Commander Karnavas could get us the week for the following week, that would be helpful for us as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's what I'm going to say on this particular issue. Well, it's time for a break and we'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa, any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to start off with a few questions that relate to how long you've known Colonel Blagojevic. Can you tell us that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: From the time he was appointed up until the time I was demobilised in 1996. So it would have been from late May 1995 until the 20th of April, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. So you didn't know him before May, before he was appointed as commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: You hadn't heard of him before that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Did Colonel Blagojevic have a nickname while he was commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, I believe you told us that at some point during May until mid-June you were in Belgrade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: In April the Dutch had an observation post near -- right outside of Srebrenica. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure which one you had in mind. There were three OPs in the area above Srebrenica -- actually, four. So I don't know which one you are referring to. There was Zalazje, Kozarica, Zeleni Jadar, and another one in the area of Bojna.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm talking about the one at Zeleni Jadar, and you're obviously telling us that you are aware that there was this observation post there at that time, isn't that right, in April of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, when you came back from Belgrade, was the observation post at Zeleni Jadar still there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: According to the information that I have, they moved 100 metres back towards Srebrenica, after the killing of police officers. After that incident, a general revolt occurred. Both civilian and military leaders were dissatisfied with the members of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Were you aware of Operation Jadar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And you were aware that the Bosnian Serb army in that operation attacked the observation post, resulting in its abandonment by the DutchBat at -- on -- which began May 31st and was abandoned about June 5th? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know whether the Bratunac Brigade was involved in the -- in this attack?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, it was not a major attack. As far as I know, Momir Nikolic was involved in negotiations. So far as I know, it was not a very serious countdown or attack. I don't think that fire was opened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, the question was, sir: Do you know whether the Bratunac Brigade was involved in the attack?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: It's a very general question. Attack involves both direct attacks and infantry fighting. And according to the information that I have, there was no direct conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, wasn't it an attack such that it caused the DutchBat to actually leave the post, to abandon it? Wasn't it to such a significant degree that they would abandon the post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: According to the information that I have, right above UNPROFOR there were forces of Bosnian Muslims. Our unit caused the Bosnian forces to move. And the UN checkpoint was in a semi-encirclement in the control of the VRS forces, because above the checkpoint to the east or the south-east of the checkpoint were the positions of Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. When you said it was in the control of the VRS forces, did that include the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Partly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So what you're telling us is that the Bratunac Brigade were, in fact, involved in the Jadar operation. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to go back to what was discussed in the latter part of the examination-in-chief. I understand you identified from the photograph two of your men, Milomir Tanasijevic and somebody called Zivanovic as being at Potocari on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, by way of reminder maybe we can take a look at that photograph, it's at P22, chapter 16, page 1. Now, the gentleman in the centre sitting out on the top of the APC that's marked as number 2, that was Milomir Tanasijevic. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you. And who is the other gentleman that's right behind him marked number 1?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: He, too, was part of the 3rd Infantry Battalion. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, from late June 1995, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And this photograph was taken in Potocari. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. If it's in Potocari, yes. I don't think it can be contested, because here in the foreground we see these three individuals, but I cannot quite make out the background. But, yes, I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. When you were asked about these individuals in the -- at Banja Luka by the Office of the Prosecutor investigators, didn't you tell them that you weren't aware that these men were in Potocari at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No. Because they had left for Bratunac. I didn't know when they would set off as escort for this APC.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And they didn't report to you that they went to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: What about Sreten Petrovic, were you aware that he was in Potocari on the 13th of July? He was the deputy commander of the 3rd Battalion. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. But Sreten Petrovic was injured on the 9th of July, and as far as I was concerned he was out of the battalion and the brigade until the 17th of September, 1995, he was officially in therapy, undergoing treatment. According to the information that I had, he apparently remained at the Zvornik hospital. As to when and how he arrived, I don't know. It was not possible for me to have that information at the time, because officially he was wounded on the 9th of July, and as far as I was concerned he was hors de combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So he didn't report to you that he was going into Potocari at all, he didn't mention that to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: It was not possible for Sreten to report to me, because at the time I was at Pribicevac, in the area of Pribicevac, and Sreten was undergoing treatment at the Zvornik hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, he clearly wasn't undergoing treatment if he was in Potocari on 13th July, was he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I know. But I learned this only after Banja Luka, because we went together to Banja Luka. And it was only after my interview that I learned how Sreten Petrovic had ended up in Potocari on the 12th, 12th of July. Apparently he had a visit on that day, and on his own he requested to be discharged. He asked the doctor to discharge him. So he got into a car and he left Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say then that his injuries weren't so extreme, given that he would be able to leave, ask the doctor discharged him, and go to Potocari? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: I think that that was my answer to the gentleman. He had sustained gunshot wounds, but Mr. Sreten Petrovic is a very strong man of a very strong build. I think he has complete medical documentation to that effect. He, I think, left that documentation in Banja Luka, and one could clearly see that he had sustained gunshot, entry and exit, wounds. And apparently his build was such that it enabled him to be able to move, to walk again, three days later. I don't think that it would be the case with everyone, but Sreten Petrovic was able to walk after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And why wouldn't he come back to the battalion to help you in the middle of all that was going on at the time? Why was he still officially gone from the battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: He had crutches and pins. He could not be of any help. I mean, it's one thing for him to be able to walk with his left leg and with the help of his left arm, but otherwise he could not walk normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Weren't you wounded during that period as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: I was injured on the 1st of October, 1994. But in May and June, I underwent additional surgery.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Did you go to Potocari on the 12th and 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: The order of my commander was to remain at Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Was there any other reason that you didn't go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Well, I had no business at Potocari. My wish was to enter my hometown on the 11th, but not Potocari. Potocari doesn't have any meaning for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, when you were asked this question by the investigator, sir, didn't you tell them that you didn't go to Potocari because you couldn't get in, because of the police checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could have the question and then the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not necessary under cross-examination, and I do think that Mr. Karnavas knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't know that, that's my whole point. I was never trained that way and I train lawyers how to conduct cross. I would like to know what page and what line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think in the cross-examination the party has to right to put a question to this witness first and later on, if the party is not satisfied with that answer or there is some discrepancies there, then he or she should put the specific case to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, but it would be nice to have, at least for my reference, the page number so at least I could see. Because I don't have to take the Prosecutor at their bona fides. I wouldn't do that anywhere else, why would I do that over here? I'm not about to start changing my habits. I'm not saying she's mischaracterising anything, but I think common courtesy and procedure should be that I be given at least a reference so I can look at it and follow along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Issa, you are not obliged to do that, but if you could it would be of great assistance to Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I'm just trying to find the reference in my notes. I believe it would be at page 38 in the English version of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you able to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The answer is very simple. I'm here to tell the truth, so I'm not afraid of anything. That was not the question to begin with; I think the question referred to the 13th and the 14th. Why didn't I go to Potocari? My answer, if I remember it correctly, is that at the crossing, Srebrenica/Potocari, there was a military police checkpoint. And I think that that should be the exact reading of the answer. As for the 13th -- but it would -- it referred to the 13th and the 14th, not the 12th, let alone the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, sir, my question to you was relating to the 12th and the 13th. I didn't ask you anything about the 11th. If we do go to your transcript, if you would like us to do that, the question refers to the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would like to go to the transcript --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for the 13th. So my question is yes, when it comes to the 13th, not the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: The question was, sir, and this is just to clarify: On that -- didn't you tell the investigators in Banja Luka that the reason you didn't go to Potocari was because there was a police checkpoint and they didn't allow you to go through?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Not to go to Potocari, but to go through Potocari on the way to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Because that was my tasking. It had nothing to do with Potocari, but the Srebrenica/Potocari/Bratunac road. Why I didn't go to Bratunac via Potocari, that was the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on the evening of the 13th, July, you were actually -- you spent the evening in Bratunac. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, in my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you travelled through Srebrenica, Zalazje, Sase, Voljevica, and then through Bratunac. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Bjelovac, Pobrdje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And in your words to the investigator, you said you travelled through the whole town before you got home. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, in principle.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you told us today, sir, that you were aware that there were Muslim prisoners in the Vuk Karadzic school and on buses detained that night in Bratunac. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Muslim prisoners on buses and in the various schools were abused and murdered during that period, on 12 and 13 July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No, not on the 13th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, let's go to your transcript, and I'm going to give you a copy of your transcript. Now, you told us today, sir, that you knew that there were prisoners in the Vuk Karadzic school on the 13th of July. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like you to turn to page 94, starting at line 4 through 43 in your copy. And in the English translation it's page 71, around the middle of the page, through 72. And you were asked: "We know for a fact that there were thousands of Bosnian Muslim men of military-age held in that building, thousands of men." And you say: "I don't know that. It seems there were quite a large number. And if we're thinking of the same thing, it's not far from the centre, but it's not in the direction where I was going, on the way. I don't have any --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: "I don't have any need to dispute facts, but I wasn't even close. I didn't look, and I didn't see that. Question: "It's a huge number of people, though, isn't it to be in a small town, a huge number of men?" And you answer: "Yes, but if it's a closed room or closed rooms, and if I had nothing to do with that, if somebody brought them there, held them there, guarded them there, and if I don't have anything to do with that, I didn't even know." Do you remember being asked those questions and giving those answers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Just going back then, sir, to the 11th of July. On the 11th of July you said that you wanted to report to Blagojevic -- you went to report to Blagojevic personally because you had a duty to do so. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether we understand each other. To report to what, that Srebrenica had fallen? I went to take on other duties and other assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: That's right. And you went to report to him personally so that he can give you those duties and assignments. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And in fact, you had a duty to report back to Colonel Blagojevic throughout July in relation to any tasks or orders that he gave you. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you did personally report to him, either on the morning or the evening on the 14th, 15th, 16th, and 17th of July. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'd like to go to --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let me just clarify one point. Via the communications centre, so my report in actual fact -- actually, I didn't have to receive it directly from Blagojevic, but through the communications centre. The code, I would say yes, the situation is regular, and if there is any new thing that I should be informed about, then they would have informed me in due course later on, if not that would be it, through the communications centre. I didn't have to ask for Blagojevic in person; I would do it through the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: But nevertheless you did personally see Colonel Blagojevic in person on the 14th, 15th, 16th, and 17th of July, and you did report to him, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No, no. Not personally. On the 11th, yes. And probably until the 17th, I might have seen him once again. But I was given my assignments. So it was only through the communications centre that I was able to inform him that I was working according to plan or the centre would do this. I wasn't duty-bound to have a personal meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, if he asked you to report back to him in relation to a particular order that he gave you, then you would be duty-bound to do so, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the communications centre would have been sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Turning then to exhibit P483, which is the 14th July order that we saw earlier. Now, this is the order we saw earlier, sir, and I believe in your examination-in-chief, Mr. Karnavas specifically asked you about paragraph 3 of that order, which relates to your command -- as commander of the 3rd Infantry Battalion to search the terrain. Do you remember being asked some questions about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you knew about that order, didn't you, at the time? You were given this order to search the terrain, and then you explained to us what, in fact, you did in relation to it. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'd like you to please turn to the second page of that order. And if we could look at the very last line. At paragraph 7 it states: "On completion of the task, report to me at the briefing session on 17 July 1995." Did you report to Colonel Blagojevic on 17 July 1995 in relation to this task and what you -- what parts of the terrain you searched?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to remember all the dates, but if that's what it says that it was the 17th, then it was the 17th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, in fact, you did meet with him on the 17th, because that was the day that you told us about earlier where he assigned you to search the terrain in the Konjevic Polje area. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So there would be no reason for you not to discuss this order with him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Well, there would be no reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: If he asked for that, if that's what he asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, clearly he did, according to this document. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the document, yes. But as I said, it was a long time ago, so I can't really actually remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, moving on then to the 19th of July, we can refer back to that document dated 19th July.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: It's D135 for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, you were referred to earlier to paragraph 2 where it says: "The 3rd Infantry Battalion is securing the road from Glogova to Konjevic Polje." Were you aware of the mass graves at Glogova at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Did you see loaders or excavators, engineering equipment, there at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Not then, but I wasn't at Konjevic Polje then either, nor did I pass by that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Didn't you say you were near Glogova?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: In Glogova, yes, by the communications -- by the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you didn't see the mass graves that were located in Glogova?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Then, no. I heard about the graves at Glogova a long time after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: And I don't know to this day exactly where they were, because Glogova is a broad belt.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Did you see patrols of military police from the Bratunac Brigade securing the public utility workers in Glogova?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like to now go back to the 17th of July. I'm sorry I'm skipping around like this, but if we all know where we are. Now, in your examination-in-chief, sir, I believe you were asked if you knew when you were tasked with this -- with the task of going to the terrain and searching the terrain, where you ultimately met with Gavric and Jevic. And you were asked whether or not you knew what unit Jevic was part of or at least you stated you didn't know what unit Jevic was part of. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Didn't Colonel Blagojevic, when he gave you this task on the 17th of July, in fact tell you that there would be a platoon of - and I'm quoting you - as he called them "specials" who would wait for you in the region of Sandici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No. And if I can see properly, in the order it just says the 3rd and 4th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to go to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And for the record in the English translation it's at page 16, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And for you, sir, it's at page 24, lines 22 through 52. And for context, we can turn back to page 15. And for you, it would be page 20 -- page 24, line 4 through 17. And at the very bottom of page 15, in the English translation, if I can start there. You say: "So on the 17th I brought about 60 men, and that was the only time that there was a dialogue between me and Blagojevic, because I wasn't able with those men to carry out a search of the terrain. I was told that I would not be alone and that he knows that I was not able to carry out something like that, especially with that composition of manpower. An armed squad and an ambush could destroy the whole company, regardless of the fact that it's called a company. I was told that the main forces had already passed Konjevic Polje by the 11th and 12th and were going in the direction of Crni Vrh/Tuzla, so that in that case somebody had remained behind, that would be about the same or equal to my men, and my company would be about the same composition and the same quality. And I wouldn't be alone, that the people from the Workers' Battalion would be joining me. The Workers' Battalion actually never existed. There was the work obligation, though, and it would occasionally be directed to the region of the assigned units as some sort of strengthening fortification. And these were men whose average age was even 60 with reduced physical fitness." And then you say: "And that also there would be a platoon of, as he called them, 'specials,' who would wait for me in the region of Sandici." Do you recall telling the investigators that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but your question was directly about Jevic. So when you asked me, you asked me about Jevic. So I didn't know whether there would be somebody there or not, and if somebody was there whether it would be Jevic or somebody else. So I think that's where the misunderstanding lies, on that point, otherwise all the rest. And I really didn't -- but that was the 17th. I looked at the order and I see it was the 18th when we conducted the search.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. Well --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: We might be off on the day, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's allowed to finish his answer. The courtesy should be given to the witness to answer the question. He's trying to be full and complete and she's trying to impeach him. He's entitled to answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, did you finish your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, if we understand each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, the Workers' Battalion, sir, or the work obligation, as I think you put it, you knew who they were, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you knew that Mico Gavric would be meeting you there. I think Colonel Blagojevic told you that, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So the only other platoon of people that you didn't know were the specials that Colonel Blagojevic referred to. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Colonel - excuse me - Mr. Jevic testified that there were about 200 prisoners at the time that were captured, and the three children that were also captured, which I believe was referred to earlier, also said that there were prisoners in the hundreds, as opposed to the 50 that I believe you told us about. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No. What I saw in the Sandici area was certainly that many.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Plus the three teenagers, 15, 16 years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: The next day, Radika Petrovic, who was the 4th Battalion commander testified that there were three buses that he saw in the Sandici/Lolici area with -- full of men with prisoners. And he also said that each bus could carry approximately 50 men. Does that help you refresh your recollection as to how many men were captured on the 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Well, it might refresh my memory. But if Jevic says 200, I didn't actually see the buses -- or Radika. So I didn't encounter Petrovic then, nor did I stay until the end. Perhaps there was some other captured men, too. Now, this man claims 200, the three buses, 150. I'm saying that by 1800 hours, by 1800 hours, there were not more than that many, not after 1800 hours. Afterwards, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the three teenagers that were captured, you just told us they were approximately 15 and 16 years old. Isn't that right? Those were their ages?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you -- do you know what happened ultimately to the men that were captured?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: With the men, no. The males, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I just have a couple more areas, Your Honour, and I'm nearly finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Just going back very briefly, sir, when you met with Colonel Blagojevic on the 11th of July at Pribicevac you mentioned that General Krstic was there, and I believe you said: "And there was also the command of General Krstic." This was in your examination-in-chief. Was General Krstic commanding this operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Turning then to P856. I'm just going to show you a document, sir, and I'm going to ask you a couple of questions about it. If you can look at that handwritten version of the document. At the very bottom of it, sir, at the very bottom of the document, there's a signature. You see that there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Is that Colonel Blagojevic's signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a ballistics man, I don't think so. Do you mean this?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the document I believe you're holding in your right-hand. It's handwritten, not the one with the red ink on it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No, no. I can't actually say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: You must have seen Colonel Blagojevic's signature in the past, haven't you, on various orders, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you're telling us you can't recognise his signature now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Well, I just had his signature for a few minutes. I looked at it the whole morning, and now that I see this I really don't want to venture. It's not my profession. I don't want to venture into giving an express answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. At the very bottom of that document right before the signature, sir, it doesn't say anything like: "For Colonel Blagojevic." It just says his name; there's no "for" there, is there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So shouldn't this be his signature, under "military rules"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: There are two signatures here. There's a full name and surname, if I might note, and there's a shortened version of the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: I think that this shorter one is a little longer than his actual signature, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. But the question was: If there's no "for" before a signature, the word "for," shouldn't this be his signature under military rules?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Not only under military rules, but civilian rules, too, if I understand this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: If I can just ask Madam Usher to take that away so it won't be distracting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, where is -- what is Domavija in Srebrenica town. There's a place called Domavija, can you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: A hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were asked a number of questions about the Red Berets. I just have a few. As I understood what your testimony, sir, I think you said that the Red Berets were not part of the 3rd Battalion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go to another document. It's D143. And I'm going to ask to turn to page ERN 00658848. And that page has been translated; it's the second page. All right, now, sir, let's maybe start at the very top of the page. If you look at the name that is five lines down, "Simic (Tomislav) Ivan." Do you see that name there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And if you go across and you see this individual is listed as a member of the 3rd Battalion, Crveni. And I may not be pronouncing that properly, but I believe that refers to Red Berets. Doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Well, I understand what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, the answer -- I would like you to answer that question, sir. The question was: That refers to Red Berets, doesn't it? We saw that in another document before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This list, I emphasise that it was added. This is a brigade list. If you happen to have in your possession a list dated from July of the battalion, my battalion, the 3rd Infantry Battalion, then you'll see that there is not a single name from the Red Berets there at all, whereas this is the complete list. And I never contradicted the fact that people were added.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. But as we can see here, sir, just on this page alone, there are several people from the Red Berets that are listed as members of the 3rd Battalion, if you look at that page, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And that, in fact, includes Miroslav Stanojevic, that is listed as a Red Beret and member of the 3rd Battalion on this page? It's 14 lines up from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm finished with that document. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, who has control over the Red Berets, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Do you mean directly then or generally from 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: No. I mean in 1995 at the time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: In principle, I think it was the brigade command. They were the only ones who were able to deploy them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And they were given orders then by the brigade command. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Well, that's quite normal, to the Red Berets and all the four battalions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just have one question to clarify a point. If I could show the gentleman what has been marked as P165. I think this is my only copy, if you could provide it to the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, can you read that, sir, what that document is? You don't --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a list of the 3rd Infantry Battalion, the command, and the infantry companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And on that document, which is a Prosecution document, and I believe you made reference to in your early question, are the Red Berets listed on that as part of being permanent members of the 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. May I take a moment to look through the whole document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you spoke to the Prosecutors back on 29 November 2001, which you've indicated earlier was well after Mr. Blagojevic had been indicted and later on arrested, did you tell the Prosecutors or the investigators for the Prosecution back then that on the 11th and 12th you had not moved your positions as a result of an order given by Colonel Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, how does that arise out of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It arises --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And it's a leading --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It arises out of that there has been some notion that somehow on the 13th he went to Potocari. Frankly, I have not been able to find such a section that says that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, here we're talking about the 11th and the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We're not talking about the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Some background, Your Honour, because I want to go 11th, 12th, 13th, 14th, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the situation is clear on the 11th and 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may ask some questions on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is there anywhere in your statement, sir, because I can't find it, that on the 13th you went to Potocari that you recall, in reading your statement? Do you recall telling the Prosecutors that you went on the 13th to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: No. I think I cleared it up a moment ago to the lady from the Prosecution. On the 13th -- in the evening of the 13th, I arrived in Bratunac; that is not contested. But I was in Banja Luka why I had not gone via Potocari. So my objective was not Potocari on the 13th, but Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: And I thought I had made it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: That question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were asked whether you had personally met with Colonel Blagojevic on the 14th, 15th, 16th, and the 17th when you were reporting to him. Is it not a fact when you gave a statement to the Prosecution that you said that, "Each evening or each morning I personally reported to the brigade command," command, not commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I also think that I tried to clear the issue here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I take it there is a difference between reporting to the command and reporting to the commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I believe I tried to explain that. In view of the situation I had found myself in, it was enough for me to call the communications centre and to say, okay, and ask if there was anything for me. What I want to say is there was no obligation, as such. But otherwise, yes, there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And finally you were asked or, in fact, you were read a section from your statement with respect to the events on the 17th of July, 1995. In Banja Luka, did you not in fact inform the investigators for the Prosecution that Mico Gavric was there to serve as a coordinator between your men and also the Worker's brigade. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But the question that was asked here was not the same. It was worded in a different manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you did mention Jevic when you were asked questions about who else was there, you did mention him, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ZEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you did also state, did you not, that "Mico Gavric issued an order, which neither myself nor Jevic disputed that if there were prisoners" --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- if anybody was captured and all those who were surrendered voluntarily --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm making an objection, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You Honour, I'm entitled to ask the question before the objection can be raised.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, it's very leading, Your Honour. I mean, what is he doing? He's reading out from the transcript. And aside from that, it just does not arise from the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I don't think there's any disputes on this very issue. The question has been asked and asked in the direct and in the cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The intimation is that somehow this gentleman with his troops were involved in executing prisoners captured on the 17th and on the 18th. Here I'm trying to show that when he was questioned by the Prosecution, which is consistent with what Mr. Gavric said, that he was ordered by Mr. Gavric, or Mr. Gavric at least informed both him and Jevic that the prisoners were to be treated according to the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness has already testified to this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I just have one final question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were asked about the 18th and about Mr. Radika Petrovic. Right. Here you talk about the 17th. Sir, just to clear it up: How many days were you searching the terrain, physically searching, the terrain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please do not tie me to specific dates. It was a long time ago, but we spent only one day searching. Whether it was on the 17th or the 18th, I'm not sure. But I'm sure that it was only one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage, are there any documents to tender? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have D143, pending translation. I think we have, as with the other one that is already in the translation pool, if we could have it completed. It's being officially translated, but that's the document we wish to have translated. That's the Bratunac Brigade roster for July 1995. And then the other document is D141, is the handover of the supplies of the Red Berets. And we discussed that. And that was D141.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections, Ms. Issa?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the document D143, it's admitted into the evidence temporarily, pending the translations, English translations of this document. As for the other document, D141, is admitted into the evidence. On the part of the Prosecution, are there any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We received a thick bundle of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, you did, and I didn't use all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Just in case?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. The usher will show you out of the room, and we wish you a pleasant journey back home. You may go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to Your Honour for being fair and correct to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We still have more or less five minutes left. Are there any matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, just briefly, Your Honour. Mr. Karnavas has repeatedly, especially in the last few weeks, told the Court and told the witnesses what the Prosecution is trying to prove or is proving. That's - especially when it's absolutely wrong - is improper. For example, suggesting to this man that we were calling him a murderer or trying to prove that he'd murdered people in the woods, had I had evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that this man and his unit were murdering people in the woods, it would have been part of this indictment. And perhaps I can save some time by just very briefly explaining this part of the 17 July and the sweeping of the woods and the children and the removing of the people of a certain age, this is -- only the trees can tell us what happened at that point, and any honourable witnesses. But the purpose of that, and I think the Court understands, is to show the ongoing operation. We now see through this witness that Colonel Blagojevic is actually aware of which units and he's giving orders about things. So in that respect I think we're learning something almost every day from each of these witnesses. As much as I want to end this trial, I think we are learning something every day from each of these witnesses and the Prosecution's case is getting much stronger as a result. As a result I may be filing a motion for you to reconsider your initial ruling, because through Mr. Karnavas's witnesses we now have bodies in each of the classrooms of the Vuk Karadzic school. We have Mr. Blagojevic involved in different conversations and different events related to this crime. I mean, it's innumerable what the evidence is mounting on this. But the point of what I'm saying is that if he's going to be stating what our case is, he should get it right and not inflame people by suggesting we're trying things that we have not charged in the indictment but that are part of the larger picture for you to understand the charges that are in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- has stained all of the soldiers that were with the Drina Corps or anybody else that participated during that campaign. They have spread stain from top to bottom. Everyone they claim was engaged in this murder operation, everybody was engaged in ethnic cleansing. I think I got their case right on point, and the point is they want to blame every single person who was there in that vicinity. And I don't want to go any further on that. I think I have it right. If the Prosecutor wants me to write me the script what their case is because I haven't got it right, I would be more than happy to read it to the witnesses as to what their case might be. But I think I have it by now in light of their indictment. As far as their case getting stronger, we know one thing, he was indicted before they even investigated the case. He was arrested like a common criminal, like a drug dealer before they investigated the case. Now we know as of last week they were interviewing the people that made coffee in the Bratunac Brigade headquarters trying to find something on Mr. Blagojevic. And there's nothing there. The shame of it is that they went after this man, they indicted him before investigating, and it's a result-oriented Prosecution. And that's what I'm trying to present to each and every one of the witnesses and to everybody who is watching this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, as a matter of fact in most of the occasions, I say in most of the occasions, mentioning the Prosecution's case is not necessary in your question. You may cite the indictment. You may say that the indictment alleged certain matters. But frankly speaking, at this moment, we haven't formed any opinions on the Prosecution's case or on your case yet, because we haven't finished the witnesses yet. So in order to avoid unnecessary conflicts or obstacles to the proceedings, my advice is that reduce mentioning the other party's case or person to the minimum, only at necessary points. Yes. Are there any other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I have another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take the Court's advice and I appreciate that. There are two matters, both related. We're trying -- we've put on our list Colonel Karremans who wasn't called by the Prosecution or I believe in the previous cased related to this one. Also we put on Karl Bildt. The Dutch government, for whatever reason, has refused to provide us with any assistance. We've gone through the liaison person who works for the ICTY, we've gone through the Ministry of Defence. They told us that they have nothing to do with the gentleman. We've gone through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and it seems we are running against obstacle on obstacle. As with Karl Bildt, we contacted the Swedish embassy, they gave me an e-mail address. I wrote to the gentleman, we've called him again, and basically, nothing is happening. Though I believe with Mr. Bildt, he might also be wanted in the Milosevic case. I was wondering whether, in light of their situations, their positions, whether we could expect or hope for any assistance from this Tribunal. We believe that both are very critical witnesses to this finding process. So -- but I don't know whether this Trial Chamber is able to coerce or cajole, I should say, the two governments into assisting us and bringing these two gentlemen here for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we came across the same issue during the direct examination. We discussed about the testimony of one of the witnesses there, and from my experience it is very difficult to deal with the host government. But first of all I would like to say that the testimony of those witnesses that you are seeking the help should be the most critical and essential witnesses. Secondly, is that you have to exhaust all the means at your disposal. And if so, we'll consider what we could do in this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. If I might ask: Exhaustion? I mean, I'm exhausted in trying. I may not have exhausted all of my means, but I'm certainly exhausted. Where does the line end as far as exhaustion of effort go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. McCloskey is more experienced in this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I've been watching Mr. Karnavas for a long time and I haven't seen him get exhausted yet. I'm hoping, but I haven't seen that. In relation to these two witnesses, in the foundation for Karl Bildt, I don't really see the justification for calling him. Perhaps a more detailed justification would lead to something, especially as we want to end this trial at some point. I think your point is very well-taken, that we need some real reasons. And Mr. Bildt and this idea of Sarajevo and Srebrenica being traded, this is in the land of politics and conspiracy theories, which I don't think will help the Court. Now, Colonel Karremans obviously is a person that was involved. Mr. Karnavas has made a point in his documents, and it sounds, from my knowledge of it, that he has exhausted perhaps most of the remedies for getting him here. And I think the Dutch government, if they're going to want Tribunals in their country, which I know they do, ought to help out the Defence, the Prosecution, and the Court. So -- and I have no objections regarding Colonel Karremans. He is clearly someone that may assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So, Mr. Karnavas, if you want to file something, you have to state very clearly in your motion the reasons to justify that request, as we informed you before. And how about the 92 bis filings? It will take some time for the Tribunal to work in this aspect. We are expecting those filings very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm sure you are, Mr. President, Your Honours. And they are coming your way very, very soon. We have, as I understand it, virtually all of the statements have recently been translated and now we're finalising the motion itself. So we hope to have it in by next week, no doubt. I was also reminded by my colleagues on the team that it might be useful - and I'm only throwing this out as a suggestion - but it might be useful that after next week the Defence be given a week break to sort of regroup and tidy up any other matters that need to be done in the field. It is not a -- it is not a formal request, though it is a suggestion that I am throwing out at this point. By the end of next week, we would have put on 24 witnesses in total. So I haven't spoken to the Prosecution and I haven't spoken to my colleagues on the Defence, but my team members have been rather -- I don't want too vociferous, but rather emphatic about me asking of the Trial Chamber of the possibility of having a week break in order to sort of catch up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I can just briefly respond on the Prosecution's position on that. As you know, in our case we occasionally did have such a break and it was of great help because you do get very exhausted, as I know you are very tired. So I would not object, especially if Mr. Karnavas might review his witness list a little bit and maybe think about reducing it somewhat, because there's quite a bit of repetition in it, or trying to reduce it to 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think we mentioned that your case should be finished by the end of June, that is next month. And within this time, as for how many witnesses and how are you going to arrange the testimony of these witnesses is your business. We stick to the principle that one day, one witness, up to now we are satisfied with it. Although, we should anticipate that there are some longer witnesses which may -- who might take about two or three days. If you could cut short the witness list or turn some live witnesses into 92 bis witnesses, we'll seriously consider your request. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one last thing. I hope we can get a witness list for the following week -- well, for our purposes, but as Mr. Karnavas knows we try to do a last-minute search of all our records related to statements or maps. While we seldom come up with anything, we have a few times and we provide that to them. The sooner we get the names and the orders, we're able to coordinate these efforts and get materials sooner. So if I could encourage getting that two-week advance, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's a reasonable request. I hope Mr. Karnavas will bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have for next week's, and I will be looking over the next one. And hopefully we'll have it out over the weekend, an e-mail, something to notify everything, because we also need to coordinate in the field passports and what have you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. The hearing is adjourned. We'll resume next Monday at 9.00 in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: at 1.55 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 10th day of May, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
